title: Collective order reorganizes dissipation and powers an active engine
authors: Michael Riedl, Vincent Wattiez, Étienne Fodor, Jan Brugués, Francesco Romanò
abstract: Motile active matter systems, from animal groups to synthetic particles, exhibit spontaneous self-organized transitions between disordered and ordered collective states. These transitions are driven by continuous energy injection, yet how energy consumption and dissipation change during these transitions remains poorly understood due to the challenge of measuring individual energetic fluxes. Here, we introduce a minimal experimental system of synthetic motile spheres that enables the first time-resolved power-budget characterization of collective motion. We show that the transition to an ordered state is accompanied by increased locomotion efficiency and a reorganization of dissipation pathways, shifting dissipation from internal friction to external slip with the environment. Leveraging this energetic reorganization, we construct an active engine powered by collective motion, capable of performing mechanical work against an external load. These findings establish energetic fluxes as quantitative observables for understanding collective state transitions and demonstrate how collective order can be harnessed for work extraction in active matter.
summary: This work experimentally investigates how collective order emerges in active matter systems by performing a detailed power budget analysis. It demonstrates that the transition to an ordered state reorganizes energy dissipation, shifting energy loss to the environment. This reorganization allows the collective motion to function as a measurable active engine capable of performing external mechanical work.
main_problem: The study aims to understand how energy consumption and dissipation change when motile active matter systems transition between disordered and ordered collective states.
main_result: The transition to an ordered state reorganizes dissipation pathways, shifting energy loss from internal friction to external slip, which allows the collective motion to power an active engine capable of performing mechanical work.
method: The researchers used a minimal experimental system of synthetic motile spheres to perform time-resolved power-budget characterization, linking energy input, dissipation, and mechanical work output.
model_or_system: The system consists of synthetic motile spheres, each equipped with an unbalanced motor, which exhibit collective transitions between disordered and ordered states. The analysis involves measuring electrical power input, kinetic energy, and decomposing total dissipation into internal and external slip components.
key_observables: Locomotion efficiency, instantaneous electrical power ($P_{el}$), kinetic energy ($P_{kin}$), internal dissipation ($P_{internal}$), external slip dissipation ($P_{slip}$), and measurable mechanical work output.
important_parameters: Motor parameters, restitution coefficient ($\epsilon$), external load applied to the engine, and the degree of collective order (e.g., rotational order parameter).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the power balance equation ($P_{el} = P_{diss} + P_{kin}$), and the engine demonstration assumes the collective forcing can be rectified by a mechanical ratchet.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the transition visualization (kymographs), the decomposition of dissipation pathways (internal vs. slip), the comparison of power budgets between collective and independent spheres, and the final demonstration of the active engine lifting an external load.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the energetic challenge in active matter, then presents the experimental setup and power budget measurements to show energy reorganization upon ordering. Finally, it leverages this reorganization to construct and test a mechanical active engine.
why_interesting: The concept of harnessing collective energy reorganization to perform directed work is highly relevant to non-equilibrium statistical mechanics and active matter theory, providing quantitative metrics for state transitions beyond simple energy conservation.
